opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a great question, because there's a tempting line of thinking that goes, "Well, if an agent can just write whatever glue code you need on the fly, why bother designing interfaces carefully at all?" But I actually think it goes the other way. The easier it gets to generate code, the more the interfaces between pieces of code matter.

Part of it is just that a protocol is a social contract, not only a technical artifact. When you define an API, you're making a promise to everyone who depends on it: here's what this call means, here's what happens when it fails, here's what stays stable over time. You can vibe code a client in five minutes, but if the thing on the other side changes its semantics every week, or two systems disagree on what a field means, all that generated code is wrong in subtle ways. Code generation doesn't fix ambiguity. It amplifies it, because now you have a hundred slightly different interpretations instead of one.

The second piece is that the hard parts of systems were never really the typing. They're things like consistency, failure handling, security boundaries, versioning, and performance under load. If you think about what made something like SQL or HTTP or even Parquet last, it wasn't that the implementation was clever. It's that someone thought hard about the abstraction: what you expose, what you hide, what guarantees you give. Those decisions compound for decades. A model can help you explore that design space faster, but somebody still has to decide what the contract is and stand behind it.

And third, agents are actually going to be the biggest consumers of these interfaces. If you have lots of agents calling tools and services, you really want those tools to be well specified, predictable, with clear error semantics and permissions. A sloppy API is annoying for a human developer; for an agent operating at scale, it's a reliability and security problem. So I'd argue good protocol design becomes more valuable, not less. It's the part that lets all this cheap, fast-generated code actually compose into something you can trust.

r001.rationale: The response says APIs promise stable semantics and that changes can break dependent code, but it does not explain coordination between systems that evolve at different speeds.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's actually a kind of paradox here, which is that the easier it gets to generate code, the more valuable the interfaces between pieces of code become. When writing software was expensive, the API was almost a byproduct. You built a system and you exposed whatever happened to be convenient. Now the code inside a component is cheap, almost disposable. You can regenerate it, you can have an agent rewrite it overnight. But the contract between components is the thing everyone else depends on, and that's exactly the thing you can't regenerate without breaking the world around it.

I think about it like the difference between a building and the plumbing standards. You can tear down and rebuild a house pretty quickly these days. But the fact that the pipes are a standard diameter and the electrical outlets are a standard shape is what lets anyone build anything at all. Protocols are the shared coordination layer. They're a social artifact as much as a technical one. And agents writing code on demand don't resolve the social problem. If anything they make it worse, because now you have far more code being produced by far more parties, and they all need to agree on something to interoperate.

The other piece is that the interface is where the hard decisions actually live. What's the unit of work? What's the failure semantics? How do you version it, how do you handle a partial result, what's idempotent? A model can give you something that works for the happy path in thirty seconds. But a lot of what makes an API good is the stuff you only learn after it's been in production for two years and someone's built a business on a corner case you didn't think about. That accumulated judgment doesn't come for free from a prompt. You have to decide what you're committing to.

And honestly, we've seen this already in the agent space. Something like MCP exists not because anyone couldn't write the glue code. Every team could vibe code an integration to every tool in an afternoon. It exists because N-squared bespoke integrations is a terrible equilibrium, and you want one deliberately designed surface that everyone builds against. The faster code generation gets, the more I think the scarce skill shifts toward deciding what the boundaries should be, and being disciplined enough not to move them every week.

r001.rationale: The response describes APIs as a shared coordination layer for parties that need to interoperate, but does not say their systems evolve at different speeds.

r002.rationale: It discusses agent integrations and shared standards, but does not draw the requested comparison to cross-company data sharing or explicitly connect interoperability among agents, users, and tools.

astra-6.text:
I think generating code and agreeing on how systems should interact are different problems. You can vibe code both sides of an interface, but you still have to decide what that interface means. What happens when a request fails? Can you safely retry it? Who has permission to do what? Those decisions don’t go away because writing the implementation gets easier.

In fact, if we’re going to have agents creating lots of software on demand, good protocols become more valuable. You want each new application to plug into existing systems without having to rediscover all their assumptions. A well-designed API gives you a contract that you can test and reason about.

So I think the scarce thing shifts a little bit. It’s less about typing out the code and more about choosing the right abstractions and semantics—especially when different people, or different agents, are building pieces independently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between generating an implementation and deciding what the contract should be. You can generate code very quickly, but that doesn't tell you what guarantees another system can rely on. What happens when a request fails? Can you retry it safely? How do permissions work? Those are still design decisions.

And, actually, if we're going to have agents building lots of software on demand, those contracts become even more valuable. You need some stable way for all these independently generated pieces to interact. An agent can figure out a complicated API, but it still benefits from an API with clear semantics.

So I think the work shifts a little bit. The implementation becomes cheaper, and choosing the right abstractions—and making them reliable enough that other people or agents can build on them—becomes a bigger part of the value.
